essays.question: Do the advantages of globalization outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons and examples.

versions.text:
Goods, money and ideas now cross borders faster than ever, and the question is whether the advantages of globalisation outweigh the disadvantages. This essay will discuss both sides before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, globalisation raises growth and choice. Open markets bring cheaper goods, investment and technology. A consumer who buys a phone assembled in Asia with parts from several continents, for example, pays much less than she would if every part were made locally. Developing countries have attracted factories and created jobs, and millions of people have escaped poverty through export industries. Companies can reach larger markets, which allows them to grow, and universities and scientists share knowledge across the world. Cultural exchange also brings new food, music and ideas into people's daily lives.

On the negative side, globalisation creates losers and cultural pressure. Workers in uncompetitive industries lose jobs, small firms struggle against multinationals and local cultures may fade. A town whose factory closes because production has moved to a country with lower wages, for example, may suffer for decades. Global supply chains spread diseases, financial crises and pollution, and countries that depend on imports become vulnerable when trade is disrupted. Large companies may also avoid taxes and pay low wages. Nevertheless, these problems can be reduced by retraining schemes, fair labour and environmental standards and international cooperation. Gains must be shared through retraining and fair rules.

In conclusion, globalisation has brought substantial benefits in growth, choice and knowledge. On balance, I believe that the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, provided that governments protect workers and communities who are harmed by change.

essays.question: Some people prefer small local shops while others prefer large supermarkets. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Every town has a choice between a corner shop where the owner knows the customers and a large supermarket with hundreds of products, and opinions differ on which is preferable. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of small local shops argue that they offer personal service and community links. Small shops know their customers and keep money in the area. A grocer who remembers that an elderly neighbour cannot carry heavy bags, for example, may deliver her shopping and keep an eye on her health. Local shops often sell fresh produce from nearby farms, support local jobs and make streets lively, and the owners are more likely to sponsor local sports and festivals. Shopping is quicker for those who live close by, and walking to the shop reduces the need to drive.

On the other hand, supporters of supermarkets argue that they provide low prices and choice. Supermarkets buy in bulk, stock thousands of products and open long hours. A busy family who can buy food, clothes and household items in one trip at a low price, for example, saves both time and money. They also offer car parks, ready meals and loyalty discounts, and many are open until late at night, which suits people who work long hours. Competition between supermarkets keeps prices low, which helps families on tight budgets. However, large stores can drive small shops out of business and often pay suppliers less.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that a mix serves different needs: supermarkets are practical for the weekly shop, but local shops deserve support because they strengthen the community.

essays.question: Some believe that private companies should pay more taxes. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
Governments need money for hospitals, schools and roads, and some believe that private companies should pay more taxes. I agree to a large extent, since companies benefit from public services and should contribute fairly, although very high rates can reduce investment.

To begin with, companies should pay a fair share of tax. Firms use roads, courts and educated workers, so their taxes pay for them. A factory that depends on a highway to deliver goods and on local schools to produce skilled staff, for example, gains from public spending and should help to finance it. Many large companies pay far less than individuals do, because they use accounting arrangements to move profits to low-tax countries. Higher contributions from them would reduce the burden on ordinary workers and allow governments to improve services without raising personal taxes. Public trust also increases when citizens see that powerful firms pay their way.

However, excessive rates may discourage expansion or push profits abroad. If taxes are too high, firms may hire fewer people, raise prices or move their headquarters to countries with lower rates. A start-up that needs every pound to grow, for example, could be harmed by heavy taxation before it makes any profit. Closing loopholes matters more than higher rates. Governments should ensure that existing rules are applied, prevent artificial transfers of profit and cooperate internationally to set a minimum rate, while offering incentives for research and investment. Small companies may need lower rates than large multinationals, which have greater ability to pay.

In conclusion, I agree that private companies should pay more tax, provided that the system is fair and does not discourage genuine investment.

essays.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of raising the minimum wage.

versions.text:
Several countries have raised their minimum wage in recent years, and this essay will discuss the advantages and disadvantages of raising the minimum wage before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, a higher minimum wage lifts incomes. Low-paid workers gain purchasing power and motivation. A cleaner or a shop assistant who earns more, for example, can pay rent, buy food and perhaps save a little, instead of working two jobs to survive. The extra money is mostly spent locally, which increases demand and supports businesses in poor areas. Governments also save on benefits, since fewer working families need support. Better pay reduces staff turnover, which lowers recruitment and training costs for employers, and it makes work more attractive than unemployment. Many people believe that a full-time job should provide a living income.

On the negative side, a higher minimum wage may raise business costs. Small firms may cut hours, raise prices or replace workers with machines. A small café that has to pay more to each employee, for example, may hire fewer staff or close early, which reduces opportunities for young people and the unskilled, who need experience most. Prices of services may rise, so that part of the gain is lost. Some economists argue that the increase can cause unemployment, although evidence suggests that moderate increases have limited effects. Moderate, gradual rises work best, together with tax relief for small firms and training for low-skilled workers.

In conclusion, raising the minimum wage has significant benefits for low earners, but it must be handled carefully. On balance, I believe that the advantages outweigh the disadvantages when increases are moderate and introduced step by step.

essays.question: What are the causes of urban poverty? What solutions can be proposed?

versions.text:
In many cities, families live in crowded slums only a few kilometres from glittering towers, and this essay will discuss the causes of urban poverty and suggest solutions, focusing on work and housing.

To begin with, urban poverty comes from insecure work, costly housing and low skills. Migrants and low earners pay high rents for unstable jobs. A young man who arrives from the countryside without qualifications, for example, may find only casual work on building sites, earn too little to rent a decent room and end up sharing a crowded space with strangers. Without a secure contract, he has no sick pay or savings, and one illness can push the family into debt. Poor schools in deprived districts and the cost of transport to distant jobs add to the cycle. Cities also attract more workers than the formal economy can employ, so many are forced into the informal sector, where wages are low and conditions are unsafe.

In terms of solutions, affordable homes, vocational training, fair wages and services in poor districts help people to escape poverty. Governments can build social housing and improve slums with water, electricity and sanitation, while setting a minimum wage and enforcing contracts to protect workers. Training centres that teach construction, computing or care skills, for example, allow unemployed adults to find better jobs. Public transport links reduce the time and cost of getting to work, and microloans help small traders. Investment in schools and clinics in poor districts gives children better chances. Such policies replace dependency with opportunity.

In conclusion, urban poverty arises from insecure work, expensive housing and low skills, and it can be tackled through housing, training and decent wages.

essays.question: Some people believe that immigration brings economic and cultural benefits. Others think it causes problems. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
People move across borders for work, study and safety, and opinions differ on whether immigration brings economic and cultural benefits or causes problems. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of immigration argue that it brings economic and cultural benefits. Migrants fill labour shortages, pay taxes and start businesses while enriching food, art and ideas. A nurse who moves from another country, for example, may fill a vacancy that local graduates cannot, and an immigrant who opens a restaurant creates jobs and offers new tastes to the neighbourhood. Many migrants are young and of working age, which helps countries with ageing populations to pay for pensions and health care. Cities that welcome newcomers, such as London and Toronto, are often centres of creativity and trade, because diverse people share different skills and perspectives.

On the other hand, critics argue that rapid arrival can strain housing and services and cause social tension. Schools and hospitals may struggle to cope when numbers rise suddenly, and local workers may feel that they compete for low-paid jobs. In some areas, language differences and separate communities lead to misunderstanding and mistrust. A town whose population grows by a fifth in two years, for example, may find that rents rise and public services are overwhelmed. Integration policy decides the outcome. Language courses, fair access to work, investment in housing and clear rules help newcomers to join society and reduce conflict.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that well-managed immigration brings more benefits than problems, but governments must plan for integration and for the pressure on public services.

essays.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using drones in delivery services.

versions.text:
Small flying machines that carry parcels, medicines and food are being tested in several countries, and this essay will discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using drones in delivery services before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, delivery drones are fast and reach remote places. They avoid traffic and can carry medicines to villages. A drone that delivers blood to a rural clinic across a river, for example, can complete in fifteen minutes a journey that would take hours by road, and it may save a life. Drones produce fewer emissions than vans for short trips, and they can reduce the number of lorries in city streets. For companies, they cut labour and fuel costs once the system is established. Customers benefit from rapid service, and drones also help in emergencies such as floods, when roads are blocked.

On the negative side, drones are limited by load, safety and noise. Small payloads, battery range, accidents and privacy issues limit their use. A drone can carry only a few kilograms for a short distance, so it is unsuitable for furniture or large grocery orders. Noise disturbs residents, and a falling drone may injure people or damage property, especially in crowded areas. Cameras on drones raise concerns about privacy, and rules on airspace are still developing. Weather such as strong wind or rain can ground the machines. Nevertheless, with clear regulations, designated routes and improved batteries, many of these problems can be managed. They suit special cases rather than all deliveries.

In conclusion, drones offer speed and access in specific situations. On balance, I believe that the advantages outweigh the disadvantages for urgent and remote deliveries, but they will not replace conventional vehicles.

essays.question: Many people think that online reviews influence buying decisions. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Before buying a phone, a hotel room or a restaurant meal, most people now read the stars and comments left by other customers, and many think that online reviews influence buying decisions. I agree with this view, since shoppers trust the experience of other buyers, although some reviews are unreliable.

To begin with, online reviews strongly influence purchases because shoppers trust the experience of other buyers. Star ratings and comments reduce the risk of a poor purchase. A traveller who sees that a hotel has a rating of four and a half stars from two thousand guests, for example, will probably book it rather than a similar one with a lower score. Reviews supply details that advertising does not, such as noise at night, the quality of service or the size of a room, and they come from people who have no reason to sell. Shops that have a high rating attract more customers, and platforms rank products according to ratings, which increases their visibility. Surveys show that most consumers read reviews before they buy.

However, fake or paid reviews can mislead, so careful readers check many sources. Some companies pay people to write praise or post false criticism of competitors, and a few customers write extreme comments because they are angry or have received a free gift. A reader who looks only at the average score may therefore be deceived. Sensible shoppers read several detailed reviews, look for repeated points and consider the number of ratings and the date. Platforms should detect and remove false reviews, and authorities can fine companies that cheat. Businesses must protect their ratings by keeping standards high and by responding politely to complaints, since public opinion online has become a major factor in their success.

In conclusion, I agree that online reviews influence buying decisions, but consumers should read them critically.

essays.question: How far do you think online shopping will change retail in the next 20 years? Support your answer with reasons.

versions.text:
Parcels arrive at doors every day, and many shopping streets have empty units, so the question is how far online shopping will change retail within twenty years. I believe that it will transform retail greatly, although physical shops will survive as experience centres.

To begin with, convenience, price comparison and home delivery draw customers online. Shoppers can buy anything at any hour, compare prices in seconds and have the goods brought to their door. A busy parent who orders groceries, clothes and a birthday present in one evening, for example, saves hours of travel and queues. Companies without shops can sell at lower prices, because they save on rent and staff, and new technologies such as virtual fitting rooms and faster delivery will make online purchases even more attractive. Many chains have already closed branches, and the share of internet sales continues to rise each year, especially among young consumers.

However, people still want to try clothes, see goods and enjoy shopping as a social activity. Some products, such as fresh food, furniture and luxury items, are better judged in person, and returns of unsuitable goods are a nuisance and a cost. Shops that offer expert advice, comfortable surroundings and events can attract visitors, and many online companies are opening physical stores to build trust. Retailers will therefore combine online and in-store services, for example by letting customers order on a website and collect goods at the shop. The high street will become smaller but more focused on experience, while delivery and warehouses will expand.

In conclusion, online shopping will change retail to a very large extent over the next twenty years, but physical shops will not disappear.

essays.question: Some people believe that immigration benefits economies. Others disagree. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Economists and politicians often argue about the effects of newcomers on a country's economy, and opinions differ on whether immigration benefits economies. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters argue that immigration benefits economies in several ways. Migrants fill labour shortages, pay taxes and start businesses. A country with an ageing population, for example, needs young workers in hospitals, farms and construction to support its pensioners. Many entrepreneurs, from small shop owners to founders of technology companies, are migrants, and they create jobs for local people as well. Skilled immigrants bring knowledge and links to foreign markets, while migrants who send money home or return to their countries of origin build trade networks. Studies from several countries show that, on average, immigrants contribute more in taxes than they receive in benefits.

On the other hand, critics argue that immigration can harm parts of the economy. Rapid arrival can strain housing and services, and low-skilled workers may face more competition for jobs and lower wages. A town where many new residents arrive in a short time, for example, may find that rents increase and schools become overcrowded before new capacity is built. Employers may also prefer cheaper foreign workers, which weakens incentives to train local staff. Some countries lose skilled workers through emigration, which is a problem for the countries of origin. Nevertheless, careful policies reduce these effects. Governments can match visas to labour needs, invest in housing and schools in areas that receive many migrants and enforce labour standards so that no group of workers is undercut.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that immigration generally benefits economies, provided that it is managed and that local communities receive support.

essays.question: Some argue that lowering taxes stimulates the economy. To what extent do you agree?

versions.text:
Governments facing weak growth often promise tax cuts, and some argue that lowering taxes stimulates the economy. I agree to a limited extent, since tax cuts can encourage spending and investment, but the effect depends on who benefits and how the lost revenue is replaced.

To begin with, lower taxes can stimulate spending and investment. Households and firms with more money may spend or hire. A family that pays less income tax, for example, may buy a car or home improvements, which creates demand for local businesses and jobs. Lower taxes on company profits can encourage firms to expand, buy equipment or start new projects, and a lower tax rate can attract foreign investors. In a recession, when demand is weak, a temporary reduction in sales tax can persuade consumers to buy sooner, giving the economy a quick boost. Lower taxes on work may also encourage people to take jobs or to work longer hours.

However, the effect depends on who benefits and on how deficits are financed. Wealthy savers may not spend the extra money, and lost revenue can mean cuts in services such as schools and hospitals or higher government debt, which must be repaid later. A broad cut that mainly helps high earners, for example, may raise inequality without much increase in demand. Targeted cuts work better than broad ones: tax relief for low and middle earners, who spend most of what they receive, and incentives for investment in productive equipment give more benefit per unit of lost revenue. Evidence from different countries shows mixed results, so tax policy should be judged by its results.

In conclusion, lowering taxes stimulates the economy only to a limited extent, and governments should design cuts carefully and keep public finances sustainable.

essays.question: Discuss how corporate social responsibility affects consumer choices.

versions.text:
Many supermarket shelves carry products labelled fair trade, organic or recycled, and this essay will discuss how corporate social responsibility affects consumer choices, focusing on ethical preferences and on trust.

To begin with, corporate social responsibility shapes consumer choice because many shoppers prefer ethical brands. Customers reward companies that treat workers fairly and protect the environment. A shopper who has two similar pairs of trainers at similar prices, for example, may choose the one made by a brand that publishes its factory standards and uses recycled materials. Surveys show that many people, especially the young, are willing to pay a little more for products that are ethical, and they may stop buying from companies that are connected with child labour or pollution. Strong programmes also build loyalty, since customers feel that they share the company's values and are contributing to a good cause.

However, greenwashing and higher prices can limit the effect. Some companies advertise small ethical gestures while continuing harmful practices, which makes consumers cynical, and families on tight budgets cannot always afford more expensive goods. Honest, visible responsibility builds loyalty. Firms must back their claims with independent certification, clear reports and real changes in their supply chains, and governments can punish false claims. Consumers should look for trusted labels and ask questions before they buy. When companies and shoppers both take responsibility seriously, ethical behaviour becomes an advantage in the market rather than a cost.

In conclusion, corporate social responsibility influences consumer choices considerably, particularly where it is genuine and well communicated.

essays.question: Do the advantages of a cashless society outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons and examples.

versions.text:
Contactless cards, mobile wallets and online transfers have made banknotes less common, and the question is whether the advantages of a cashless society outweigh the disadvantages. This essay will discuss both sides before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, a cashless society is fast and traceable. Cards and apps speed up payments and reduce theft and tax evasion. A shopper who taps a phone at the till, for example, finishes in seconds, and a street trader who accepts digital payments does not have to carry large sums of cash that might be stolen. Every transaction leaves a record, so it is more difficult to hide income or to launder criminal money, which increases tax revenue. Governments save on printing, transporting and protecting banknotes and coins, and businesses spend less time counting money at the end of the day. Digital payments also make online shopping and international transfers easy.

On the negative side, it excludes some people and weakens privacy. Elderly or poor people may lack bank accounts or smartphones, outages leave shoppers stranded and every purchase is recorded. A person whose card is blocked or whose phone battery dies, for example, cannot buy food, and a power cut can paralyse an entire shopping street. Cyberattacks and fraud are also serious risks, and spending data may be misused by companies or authorities. Cash allows people to budget and to pay anonymously. Cash should remain an option. A balanced approach would encourage digital payment while protecting access to cash for those who need it and ensuring that systems are secure and private.

In conclusion, a cashless society offers convenience and efficiency, but its drawbacks are significant. On balance, I believe that the advantages outweigh the disadvantages only if cash remains available and privacy is protected.

essays.question: To what extent should governments support small businesses? Give reasons for your answer.

versions.text:
Corner shops, workshops and family restaurants make up most of the businesses in many countries, and the question is to what extent governments should support small businesses. I agree to a large extent, since small firms create jobs and local prosperity, although support should not become permanent dependency.

To begin with, governments should support small businesses because they create most jobs and local prosperity. Small firms provide a large share of employment and innovation, yet they face higher borrowing costs and more paperwork than large companies. A baker who wants to buy a second oven, for example, may be refused a loan because the bank sees the risk as too high, and she may spend days filling in tax forms that large firms handle with a department. Small businesses keep money in local communities, create opportunities for young people and diversify the economy so that it depends less on a few giant employers. In rural areas and poorer districts, they are often the only source of work.

However, support should aim to build resilience, not permanent dependency. If firms receive endless subsidies, they may stay inefficient and avoid improvement, and taxpayers pay for businesses that cannot survive. Support should therefore be targeted and temporary: guarantees for loans, simpler registration and accounting, advice, training and public contracts that are open to small suppliers. Governments should also remove barriers such as complicated regulations rather than only giving money. Evaluation of programmes helps to make sure that public funds produce results. When help encourages firms to grow and compete, the whole economy benefits.

In conclusion, I agree that governments should support small businesses to a large extent, provided that assistance is targeted and encourages independence.

essays.question: Some people believe that tax incentives encourage innovation. Others think not. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Governments often cut taxes for firms that invest in research, and opinions differ on whether tax incentives encourage innovation. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters argue that tax incentives encourage innovation. Credits reduce the cost of research and attract firms. A pharmaceutical company that can deduct part of its laboratory spending from its tax bill, for example, may decide to hire more scientists and test more drugs. Because new ideas often benefit society more than the firm that produces them, public support can correct this imbalance. Countries such as Ireland and Singapore have used low taxes and research credits to attract technology companies and to create highly skilled jobs. Incentives are also simple to administer compared with grants, and they allow businesses rather than officials to choose projects.

On the other hand, critics argue that incentives do not guarantee innovation. Companies may claim them for work that they would have done anyway, and the lost revenue is spent on activities that produce no new ideas. A large firm that relabels routine product tests as research, for example, receives a tax benefit without improving anything. Tax breaks mainly help profitable firms, while start-ups with no profits gain little. Direct grants, public laboratories and links with universities can be more effective and easier to focus on important problems. Incentives need clear targets and review. Governments should define research carefully, check that claims are genuine, cap benefits and evaluate whether the spending actually leads to patents, products and jobs.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that tax incentives can help innovation, but only when they are well designed and combined with direct support for research.

essays.question: Many people think that influencer marketing misleads consumers. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Ordinary users who gain millions of followers are now paid by brands to recommend products, and many people think that influencer marketing misleads consumers. I agree to a large extent, since sponsorship is often hidden and claims are exaggerated, although some influencers are honest.

To begin with, influencer marketing can mislead consumers when sponsorship is hidden or claims are exaggerated. Followers trust influencers as friends, so undisclosed payments make recommendations look sincere. A beauty influencer who shows a new cream and says that it changed her skin in a week, for example, may have been paid and given the product free, and the improvement may result from lighting and filters. Posts that look like personal opinions are often scripted by advertising agencies. Young followers in particular may not realise that they are watching an advertisement, and they may buy products that they do not need or that do not work as promised. Some influencers promote financial schemes or supplements without any expertise, which can cause real damage.

However, not all influencers are dishonest. Many state clearly when a post is sponsored, test products before recommending them and refuse offers that do not fit their values. A cooking channel that explains why it uses a certain brand of knife, and mentions the free sample, for example, gives useful information. Disclosure rules protect buyers. Authorities can require labels such as "advert" or "paid partnership" on every sponsored post, punish false claims and educate young people on how influencer marketing works. Platforms can also build tools that mark paid content automatically. Consumers should treat recommendations as one source among many and read independent reviews.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that influencer marketing misleads consumers, but clear rules and critical attitudes can reduce the problem.

essays.question: Do the advantages of privatizing services outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons and examples.

versions.text:
Governments in many countries have sold or are considering selling services such as railways, water supply and prisons to private companies, and the question is whether the advantages of privatising services outweigh the disadvantages. This essay will discuss both sides before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, privatising services can raise efficiency. Competition and profit motives encourage cost control and innovation. A railway operator that wants to attract passengers, for example, may introduce better timetables, cleaner trains and online booking, because it loses money if customers go elsewhere. Private firms can raise capital from investors, which allows them to modernise equipment faster than a government with limited budgets. The state saves money when it no longer has to pay for losses, and it can concentrate on regulation and on core tasks such as health and education. Managers in private companies can also dismiss poor performers more easily, which improves quality.

On the negative side, private firms may raise prices, ignore unprofitable areas and form monopolies. A private water company that serves a remote village at a loss, for example, may stop doing so, leaving residents without an essential service. Where there is no real competition, as with pipes or rails, firms can charge high prices and reduce investment while paying large dividends. Workers may face job cuts and lower pay. Strong regulators and clear service duties are essential. Governments should set quality standards, cap prices, require service to all areas and be ready to take control if a company fails.

In conclusion, privatisation can improve efficiency but also threatens access and fairness. On balance, I believe that the disadvantages outweigh the advantages for essential services, although privatisation can be suitable for activities where real competition exists.

essays.question: Many people say that tackling poverty requires international cooperation. Do you agree or disagree? Give reasons and examples.

versions.text:
Hunger, disease and lack of schooling affect hundreds of millions of people, and many people say that tackling poverty requires international cooperation. I agree with this view, since the causes of poverty cross borders, although each country must also act at home.

To begin with, tackling poverty needs international cooperation because its causes cross borders. Trade rules, debt, climate change and disease affect poor countries more than they can handle alone. A small farming nation whose crops are destroyed by drought caused by global warming, for example, cannot solve the problem by itself, and a pandemic spreads quickly from one country to another. Rich nations can offer aid, debt relief and technology, and international organisations can coordinate responses to disasters and share knowledge about successful programmes, such as vaccination and school meals. Fair trade rules that open markets to poor countries allow them to sell their goods and earn money. Without cooperation, poor countries may remain trapped.

However, each government must also take responsibility at home. Good governance, honest institutions, investment in education and health, and policies that encourage business are essential, and aid can be wasted where corruption is widespread. Countries such as South Korea and Vietnam improved living standards mainly through their own policies, with outside support playing a secondary role. Joint action multiplies local effort. Aid should therefore be targeted, transparent and designed together with the recipients, and it should aim to build skills and institutions that make dependency unnecessary. Individuals and charities also help through donations and volunteering.

In conclusion, I agree that tackling poverty requires international cooperation, but its success depends equally on responsible policies within each country.

essays.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of banking online.

versions.text:
More and more customers pay bills, transfer money and check balances on a phone instead of visiting a branch, and this essay will discuss the advantages and disadvantages of banking online before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, online banking is convenient and cheap. Customers can pay and check balances at any time. A busy employee who transfers rent on a Sunday night from his sofa, for example, saves a trip to a branch and avoids queues, and a traveller abroad can control her account without delay. Transactions are fast, many fees are lower than for counter services, and statements are available instantly, which makes it easier to monitor spending and to spot mistakes. Banks reduce costs by closing branches, and they pass on some savings through better interest rates. Alerts and budgeting tools help customers to manage their money more carefully.

On the negative side, online banking exposes users to fraud and excludes the less digital. Phishing, outages and the loss of branches and personal advice cause problems, especially for older people. A pensioner who receives a convincing email asking for his password, for example, may lose his savings in minutes, and a system failure may prevent customers from reaching their money for hours. Rural communities may be left without a branch, and people who lack internet access or confidence are forced to depend on relatives. Strong security and branch options are needed. Banks should use two-step verification, warn customers about scams, compensate victims fairly and keep some staffed branches or telephone services for those who need them.

In conclusion, online banking brings speed and convenience, but it creates new risks. On balance, I believe that the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, provided that security is strong and traditional services remain available.

essays.question: Many people think that subscription services are good value. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Music, films, software and even meals are now sold by monthly subscription, and many people think that subscription services are good value. I agree to some extent, since a fixed fee gives access to a large amount of content, although forgotten or overlapping plans waste money.

To begin with, subscriptions give good value for frequent users. A fixed fee unlocks large libraries or services. A family that pays a modest monthly sum for a streaming service, for example, can watch hundreds of films and series, whereas buying or renting the same titles individually would cost many times more. Music subscriptions give access to millions of songs on any device, and software subscriptions provide regular updates and storage. Costs are predictable and spread over the year, which helps with budgeting, and customers can cancel when their needs change, unlike a purchase. Delivery subscriptions can save money for those who shop often, since they remove charges on each order.

However, people often keep unused plans, pay for several overlapping services and own nothing at the end. A student who signs up for a free trial and forgets to cancel, for example, may pay for months without using the service. Many households subscribe to five or six streaming platforms, so that the total cost exceeds that of a single cable package, and prices often rise after the first year. Customers also lose access to their music or films as soon as they stop paying. Value depends on regular, conscious use. Consumers should review their subscriptions regularly, share family plans where allowed and cancel those that they rarely use. Companies should make cancelling simple and remind customers of renewal dates.

In conclusion, I agree to some extent that subscription services are good value, but only for those who use them regularly and manage them carefully.

essays.question: To what extent should tax revenue be used for cultural projects? Give reasons for your answer.

versions.text:
Governments collect taxes mainly to pay for hospitals, schools, defence and roads, yet they also finance museums, orchestras, festivals and historic buildings, and the question is to what extent tax revenue should be used for cultural projects. I believe that some of it should, but only after essential services are secure.

To begin with, culture deserves a share of public money because it preserves identity and benefits society. Museums, heritage sites and arts education preserve identity and attract tourists. A city that restores its old town and supports a theatre, for example, gains visitors who spend money in hotels and shops, and residents feel pride in their history. Culture also enriches education, since children who learn music, drama or art develop creativity and confidence, and free access to galleries allows poorer families to enjoy it. Private markets alone may not support activities with small audiences, such as classical music or traditional crafts, which would disappear without help.

However, hospitals, schools and housing meet more urgent needs, so culture should receive a limited, accountable share. A government that spends millions on a grand opera house while clinics lack equipment, for example, would be criticised for its priorities. Culture projects should therefore be chosen carefully, with clear aims and regular reports on costs and results. Partnerships with private donors stretch the budget: companies and individuals can sponsor exhibitions, and ticket sales and shops can raise part of the cost. Local communities should also have a say in which projects are funded, so that the money benefits ordinary people and not only an educated minority.

In conclusion, tax revenue should be used for cultural projects to a moderate extent, after essential services have been funded.

essays.question: How can governments promote ethical consumerism? Suggest practical measures.

versions.text:
Many shoppers say that they care about fair wages and the environment, yet few check how products are made, and this essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take to promote ethical consumerism, focusing on reliable information and on incentives.

To begin with, governments can promote ethical consumerism with clear labels, honest reporting and public purchasing. Shoppers need reliable information and incentives, so certified labels, supply-chain disclosure, tax breaks and ethical public procurement make responsible choices easier. A shopper who sees an official label that guarantees fair wages and low emissions, for example, can choose without reading long reports. Companies could be required to publish where their goods come from and under what conditions they are made, and false claims should be punished by fines. Governments are also major buyers of food, uniforms and furniture, so by preferring ethical suppliers, they create a large market and set an example.

In addition, authorities should reward responsible behaviour and educate the public. Lower taxes on certified fair-trade or recycled products make them cheaper than ordinary goods, while higher charges on products that cause serious harm discourage them. Schools can teach pupils about the effects of their purchases, and campaigns can show the real cost of cheap clothing or food. Equally important, governments can support small ethical producers with loans and training so that supply grows to meet demand. Over time, demand for fair and green products rises, which encourages more companies to change their methods.

In conclusion, clear labels, supply-chain transparency, fiscal incentives and education offer the most realistic way to promote ethical consumerism.

essays.question: Some people believe that corporate mergers are good for the economy. Others disagree. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Every year, large firms announce that they will merge with rivals, and opinions differ on whether corporate mergers are good for the economy. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters argue that mergers create efficient, innovative firms. Larger companies share costs, invest in research and compete abroad. Two pharmaceutical firms that merge, for example, can combine laboratories and sales networks, develop new medicines faster and reach more countries. Duplicate offices and factories can be closed, which lowers prices or raises profits, and bigger firms may find it easier to raise money for large projects. In industries that need huge investment, such as airlines or telecommunications, small companies may be unable to survive, so mergers can save businesses and jobs. National champions can also compete with giant foreign rivals.

On the other hand, critics argue that mergers may reduce competition and jobs. Fewer rivals can mean higher prices, less choice and redundancies. A merger between the two biggest supermarkets in a region, for example, may leave customers with little choice and give the new company power over suppliers, who must accept low prices. Staff may lose their jobs when departments are combined, and small competitors may be driven out. Large firms can also become complacent and slow to innovate when they face little competition. Competition authorities should approve only beneficial deals. They can require firms to sell some operations, set conditions on prices and service, or block mergers that would create a dominant position.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that mergers can benefit the economy when they increase efficiency and innovation, but regulators must prevent deals that harm competition.

essays.question: Some people prefer to save money while others prefer to spend freely. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Some people put aside part of every salary, while others enjoy their money as they earn it, and opinions differ on whether it is better to save or to spend freely. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of saving argue that it brings security. Savers can meet emergencies and long-term goals. A family with several months of income in the bank, for example, can survive the loss of a job or an unexpected hospital bill without borrowing, and they can pay a deposit on a home or finance their children's education. Saving encourages discipline and reduces stress, because people feel more in control of their future. In old age, savings supplement a pension. Money that is saved and invested also provides funds for businesses to grow, so that it benefits the wider economy.

On the other hand, supporters of spending argue that life should be enjoyed now and that spending supports the economy. Those who never spend miss experiences, and nobody can be sure that they will live to enjoy their savings. A young couple who use their money to travel together, for example, create memories that last for life. Spending also supports shops, restaurants and jobs, and when consumers cut back too much, the economy slows. However, heavy spenders risk debt, and a sudden loss of income can lead to serious difficulty. A budget with both is most sensible. Many financial advisers suggest using a fixed share of income for needs, for wants and for saving, which allows people to enjoy the present while preparing for the future.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that a balance between saving and spending is wisest, with enough saving to be secure and enough spending to enjoy life.

essays.question: Some people believe that global trade benefits all countries. Others disagree. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Ships, planes and cables carry goods, services and money between almost every country, and opinions differ on whether global trade benefits all countries. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters argue that global trade benefits countries on average. Specialisation and larger markets raise efficiency and lower prices. A country with a warm climate that exports fruit and imports machinery, for example, can enjoy goods that it could produce only at a very high cost, and its farmers sell to millions of customers abroad. Trade brings competition, which encourages firms to improve quality and to innovate, and it gives consumers cheaper and more varied products. Many countries in East Asia grew rapidly by exporting manufactured goods and lifted millions of people out of poverty. Trade also creates links between nations that make conflict less likely.

On the other hand, critics argue that gains are uneven and some countries lose. Poorer countries may rely on raw exports with unstable prices, while the profits of processing go elsewhere. Industries that cannot compete close, workers lose their jobs and communities decline. A country that depends on selling a single crop, for example, may suffer badly when its price falls on world markets. Unequal bargaining power allows rich countries to set rules in their favour, and trade can encourage pollution and poor working conditions. Fair rules and support for losers are needed. These include trade agreements that protect labour and environmental standards, aid for developing nations to build industries and retraining for displaced workers.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that global trade benefits most countries over time, but it does not benefit all equally, so cooperation and fair rules are essential.

essays.question: How far do you think 3D printing will change manufacturing in the next 20 years? Support your answer with reasons.

versions.text:
Machines that build objects layer by layer from plastic, metal or even concrete are already used in hospitals, factories and homes, and the question is how far 3D printing will change manufacturing within twenty years. I believe that it will transform some areas greatly, although it will not replace mass production.

To begin with, 3D printing will transform prototypes, custom parts and spare supplies. It makes complex or personalised items quickly and cuts waste and transport. An engineer who wants to test a new design, for example, can print a model overnight instead of waiting weeks for a factory to make a mould. Dentists already print crowns and hearing-aid shells that fit each patient exactly, and surgeons use printed models to plan operations. Remote places such as ships, mines and space stations can print spare parts on the spot rather than carry large stocks. Because the printer adds material rather than cutting it away, less is wasted, and products can be designed in shapes that were once impossible.

However, 3D printing is slow and costly for large production runs and limited in materials. A car manufacturer that needs a million identical door handles, for example, can make them far more cheaply by casting or stamping. Printed objects are often weaker or rougher than those made by traditional methods, and only a limited range of plastics and metals can be used. Quality control and intellectual property also raise problems, since anyone with a file can copy a product. It will complement factories rather than replace them. In twenty years, printers will be common in workshops, hospitals and some homes, but most everyday goods will still come from conventional factories.

In conclusion, 3D printing will change manufacturing to a considerable extent in certain areas, but it will not replace mass production.

essays.question: Discuss the role of advertising in shaping consumer culture.

versions.text:
Billboards, television adverts and online banners surround us, and this essay will discuss the role of advertising in shaping consumer culture, focusing on the creation of wants and on its social effects.

To begin with, advertising shapes consumer culture by creating wants and defining what is fashionable. Constant messages link products to identity and success, so people buy for status. A teenager who sees a sports shoe worn by a famous player in every advertisement, for example, may feel that he needs it in order to fit in, although his old shoes still work. Advertisers use emotion, humour and attractive images to make goods appear exciting, and new models are presented as essential every year. Seasonal campaigns such as sales and gift seasons teach people to spend at certain times. Over time, this builds a culture in which shopping is a leisure activity and possessions measure personal worth.

However, advertising also has useful functions. It informs buyers about new products, prices and choices, and it makes competition between companies possible, which can lower prices. Advertising revenue pays for much of the media, from free websites to television channels. Some campaigns promote health, safety or charity, and can influence behaviour in positive ways. Consumers need critical awareness. Schools can teach young people to recognise persuasion techniques, regulators can ban misleading claims and limit advertising to children, and individuals can ask themselves whether they really need a product before buying it.

In conclusion, advertising plays a major role in shaping consumer culture by creating wants and setting social standards, although it also informs and funds the media.

essays.question: Some people prefer to use cash while others prefer digital payments. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Some shoppers pay with banknotes and coins, while others tap a card or a phone, and opinions differ on whether cash or digital payments are better. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of cash argue that it offers privacy and control. Notes work without power and make spending visible. A person who takes a fixed amount of cash to the market each week, for example, can see exactly how much is left and is less likely to overspend. Cash leaves no digital record, which protects privacy, and it can be used by people without bank accounts, such as children, tourists and the elderly. During power cuts or system failures, cash is often the only way to buy essentials. It also avoids card fees, which small traders must pay for every transaction.

On the other hand, supporters of digital payments argue that they offer speed and records. Cards and apps are faster, safer from theft and easier to track, but they depend on technology. A traveller who pays by phone abroad, for example, avoids carrying large sums and exchanging currency, and a shop assistant does not have to count change. Digital payments produce statements that help people to budget and make it harder to evade tax. They also allow online shopping and instant transfers to friends and family. However, cyberattacks, outages and the risk of overspending are drawbacks. Having both options is practical. People can use digital payments for convenience and keep some cash for emergencies and for situations where privacy or reliability matter.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I prefer digital payments for everyday use, but I believe that cash should remain widely accepted.

essays.question: Many people think that fast delivery services harm local businesses. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Parcels arrive within hours, and vans from large platforms are seen in every street, so many people think that fast delivery services harm local businesses. I agree to some extent, since large platforms attract customers away from small shops, although the same services can help independent sellers.

To begin with, fast delivery services favour large platforms. Big companies with warehouses and low prices attract shoppers away from local shops. A bookshop that sells a novel for the full price, for example, loses a customer who can order it online at a discount and receive it the next morning. Large platforms can afford loss-making offers, free delivery and returns, which small shops cannot match. As more people expect speed and convenience, high-street shops lose footfall, and many have closed, leaving empty units and reducing local employment. Money spent on the platform often leaves the community, while a local shop keeps wages and profits in the area.

However, independent businesses can use the same networks to sell more widely. A small craft maker who lists products on a marketplace and uses a courier, for example, can reach customers hundreds of kilometres away, who would never have found her shop. Local restaurants, florists and bakeries use delivery apps to attract new clients, and many shops have launched their own websites. Local firms must adapt and offer service that platforms cannot. They can provide expert advice, personal attention, unique products and fast local delivery by their own staff, and they can emphasise community links. Councils can support them by reducing business charges and improving parking and the appearance of town centres.

In conclusion, I agree to some extent that fast delivery services harm local businesses, but those that adapt can benefit from them.

essays.question: What are the benefits for a country that focuses on ethical manufacturing? Use examples.

versions.text:
Some governments encourage factories to pay fair wages, protect workers and limit pollution, and this essay will discuss the benefits for a country that focuses on ethical manufacturing, using examples such as Germany and Bangladesh.

To begin with, a country that focuses on ethical manufacturing gains reputation, skilled workers and sustainable growth. Fair wages and clean production attract responsible buyers, reduce accidents and pollution costs and build trust in exports. Germany, for example, is known for high-quality products made under strict safety and environmental rules, and many consumers are willing to pay more for goods marked "made in Germany". After a deadly factory collapse in 2013, Bangladesh introduced safety inspections and fire standards, which restored the confidence of international clothing brands. Healthy and well-paid workers are more productive and less likely to leave, so firms save on training and recruitment, and fewer accidents mean lower costs.

Furthermore, ethical manufacturing protects the environment and the community. Factories that treat waste water and reduce emissions avoid fines, cleanup costs and damage to local health and farming. Workers who earn enough support their families and spend in local markets, which stimulates the domestic economy. Companies that follow high standards find it easier to enter foreign markets with strict import rules, and investors increasingly prefer responsible firms. The main disadvantage is the higher initial cost of safer equipment and better wages, but long-term competitiveness rises as quality and reputation improve. A country can support its producers with training, loans for cleaner technology and clear, consistently enforced regulations.

In conclusion, a country that focuses on ethical manufacturing benefits through reputation, productivity, environmental protection and long-term competitiveness, despite higher initial costs.

essays.question: To what extent do you agree or disagree that brand loyalty is declining?

versions.text:
A generation ago, many families bought the same brand of soap, car or bank for decades, and some argue that brand loyalty is declining. I agree to a large extent, since shoppers compare prices and reviews easily, although strong brands still keep devoted customers.

To begin with, brand loyalty is declining in many categories because switching is easy. Online comparison, store brands and endless choice make changing simple. A shopper who sees on her phone that another brand of washing powder is cheaper and has better reviews, for example, can change within seconds, and a promotion can persuade her to try something new. Supermarkets sell their own labels that look similar to famous brands but cost less, and young consumers in particular are more willing to try new products recommended by friends or influencers. Subscriptions and apps allow customers to move from one service to another with a few taps, and economic uncertainty makes many people more careful with money.

However, strong brands with identity and loyalty programmes keep devoted customers. Some people remain committed to certain makers of phones, sports shoes or cars because the brand expresses who they are, and they accept higher prices. A person who has used the same smartphone system for ten years, for example, may stay with it because his photographs, apps and friends are connected to it. Airlines and shops use points and discounts to reward repeat purchases. Brands must earn loyalty through quality and service. Companies that treat customers well, respond quickly to complaints and keep improving their products are more likely to be trusted, and trust is more durable than a lower price.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that brand loyalty is declining, but companies with excellent products and a clear identity can still retain it.

essays.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of same-day delivery for consumers.

versions.text:
Some online retailers now promise to deliver goods within hours of an order, and this essay will discuss the advantages and disadvantages of same-day delivery for consumers before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, same-day delivery is convenient for urgent needs. Customers get goods in hours and can shop online for emergencies. A person whose washing machine breaks down on a Monday morning, for example, can order a part and have it fitted by the evening, and a parent who forgets a birthday present can still please a child on the same day. It saves travel time, particularly for people who are ill, elderly or without a car, and it allows busy workers to shop in the evening. Competition between companies has made the service cheaper than in the past, and some customers enjoy being able to track the courier on a map.

On the negative side, extra fees, fragmented trips, pollution and pressure on couriers make it less attractive in the long term. Many same-day services charge a premium for speed, which means that people pay more for goods that they could have waited for. Vans that make many small deliveries produce more emissions than a single large weekly delivery, and packaging often increases. Couriers who must meet tight deadlines may work long hours for low pay and take risks in traffic. Easy ordering also encourages impulse purchases and returns. Same-day delivery should be reserved for genuinely urgent purchases. Consumers can use standard delivery for ordinary items, group their orders and choose delivery options that are slower but cheaper and more environmentally friendly.

In conclusion, same-day delivery offers real convenience, but its costs for workers and the environment are significant. On balance, I believe that it is useful only in urgent situations.

grade.summary: Bài viết của bạn đạt chất lượng khá tốt với bố cục rõ ràng, lập luận logic và từ vựng phong phú phù hợp với chủ đề. Để đạt band điểm cao hơn, bạn cần tập trung chặt chẽ hơn vào góc độ của người tiêu dùng và tinh chỉnh một số lỗi diễn đạt nhỏ.
weaknesses: Một số ý ở đoạn nhược điểm (như điều kiện làm việc của tài xế) nghiêng về phía xã hội/người lao động hơn là trực tiếp cho người tiêu dùng.
Cách diễn đạt ở một vài câu mang tính liệt kê dài dòng thay vì phân tích sâu sắc.

feedback.taskResponse: Bài viết trả lời đúng trọng tâm đề bài, phân tích rõ cả mặt lợi và mặt hại của same-day delivery đối với người tiêu dùng. Tuy nhiên, việc đề cập đến góc độ môi trường và tài xế trong khi đề bài chỉ nhấn mạnh 'for consumers' có thể hơi lan man sang các chủ đề rộng hơn, dù vẫn có liên quan gián tiếp.
feedback.coherenceCohesion: Bố cục bài viết rất mạch lạc với các đoạn văn rõ ràng, có câu mở đầu và kết luận hoàn chỉnh. Các từ nối và phương tiện liên kết được sử dụng tự nhiên và hiệu quả.
feedback.lexicalResource: Vốn từ vựng phong phú, sử dụng tốt các cụm từ theo chủ đề như 'urgent needs', 'fragmented trips', 'impulse purchases'. Tuy nhiên, một số cụm từ còn mang tính liệt kê thay vì phát triển sâu hơn về mặt học thuật.
feedback.grammar: Cấu trúc câu đa dạng, kết hợp linh hoạt giữa câu đơn và câu phức với độ chính xác cao. Ngữ pháp vững vàng, không có lỗi lầm nghiêm trọng cản trở việc đọc hiểu.

analysis.type_vi: A/D: giao hàng trong ngày với người tiêu dùng

plan.think: Mở bài nêu nhà bán lẻ hứa giao trong vài giờ.

Tiện cho nhu cầu khẩn cấp: nhận hàng trong vài giờ; ví dụ máy giặt hỏng sáng thứ Hai đặt linh kiện, lắp tối, phụ huynh quên quà sinh nhật vẫn làm con vui; tiết kiệm thời gian cho người ốm, già, không xe; người bận mua tối; cạnh tranh rẻ hơn; theo dõi shipper trên bản đồ.

Phí, chuyến lẻ, ô nhiễm, áp lực người giao làm kém hấp dẫn dài hạn: phí cao cho tốc độ; xe giao nhiều đơn nhỏ thải nhiều hơn một đơn lớn hàng tuần, bao bì; shipper hạn chót chặt làm nhiều giờ lương thấp, rủi ro giao thông; dễ đặt gây mua bốc đồng, trả hàng; dành cho đơn khẩn cấp; giao tiêu chuẩn, gộp đơn, lựa chọn chậm rẻ hơn, thân thiện môi trường.
Chỉ hữu ích trong tình huống khẩn cấp.

essays.question: Some believe that international aid helps development. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
After earthquakes, famines and wars, rich countries send money, food and experts to poorer ones, and some believe that international aid helps development. I agree to a large extent, since aid can save lives and build services, although its success depends on how it is used.

To begin with, international aid helps development when it is targeted, transparent and builds local capacity. It saves lives in emergencies and funds clinics, schools and infrastructure. A vaccination programme financed from abroad, for example, can protect millions of children from diseases that poor governments cannot afford to fight, and a grant for rural roads or clean water allows farmers to sell their crops and families to stay healthy. Aid has contributed to major improvements in child survival and school enrolment over recent decades. Technical assistance also trains local teachers, doctors and engineers, who then continue the work without outside help.

However, corruption, dependency and poorly designed projects can waste money. If officials steal funds, or if donors give food that destroys local farmers' markets, aid may do more harm than good. Countries that receive aid for many years may stop building their own tax systems and rely on outside decisions. Some projects are chosen by donors without asking communities, and they fail when equipment breaks and no one can repair it. Aid should therefore support local ownership. Funds should be monitored and published, projects should be designed with the people who will use them, and money should go to areas such as health, education and infrastructure that create lasting benefits. Trade fairness and debt relief are also essential if poor countries are to grow.

In conclusion, I agree that international aid helps development to a large extent, provided that it is well targeted, transparent and designed with local people.

grade.summary: Bài viết có chất lượng tốt, lập luận chặt chẽ và đáp ứng tốt yêu cầu về số lượng lẫn nội dung của đề bài IELTS Writing Task 2. Người viết cần tinh chỉnh một số lỗi từ vựng và cấu trúc nhỏ để đạt điểm số cao hơn.
weaknesses: Một số diễn đạt còn mang tính liệt kê chưa đạt đến độ tinh tế của từ vựng học thuật cao cấp.
Cách dùng dấu câu trong một số câu dài có thể được tối ưu hơn để tăng độ rõ nghĩa.

feedback.taskResponse: Bài viết trả lời tốt câu hỏi, có lập trường rõ ràng (đồng tình phần lớn có điều kiện). Các ý được phát triển đầy đủ với cả mặt lợi và mặt hại, dẫn đến kết luận hợp lý.
feedback.coherenceCohesion: Bố cục rõ ràng gồm 4 đoạn với cấu trúc logic từ mở bài, thân bài (mặt lợi, mặt hại kèm điều kiện) đến kết luận. Các từ nối và phương tiện liên kết được sử dụng mượt mà.
feedback.lexicalResource: Từ vựng phong phú, sử dụng tốt các từ liên quan đến chủ đề (transparency, capacity, infrastructure, dependency). Tuy nhiên, một số cụm từ chưa thực sự tự nhiên hoặc đa dạng hơn nữa để vươn lên band cao.
feedback.grammar: Cấu trúc ngữ pháp đa dạng, sử dụng linh hoạt câu phức và câu điều kiện. Lỗi ngữ pháp rất ít, các cấu trúc câu điều kiện và mệnh đề quan hệ được kiểm soát tốt.

analysis.type_vi: Agree/Disagree: viện trợ quốc tế giúp phát triển — largely agree

plan.think: Mở bài nêu nước giàu gửi tiền, thực phẩm, chuyên gia sau động đất, nạn đói, chiến tranh; largely agree.

Giúp khi có mục tiêu, minh bạch, xây năng lực địa phương: cứu mạng khẩn cấp, tài trợ trạm y tế, trường, hạ tầng; ví dụ chương trình tiêm chủng tài trợ nước ngoài bảo vệ hàng triệu trẻ khỏi bệnh chính phủ nghèo không lo nổi; khoản cho đường nông thôn, nước sạch giúp bán nông sản, khoẻ; viện trợ góp cải thiện sống sót trẻ, đi học; hỗ trợ kỹ thuật đào tạo giáo viên, bác sĩ, kỹ sư địa phương.

Tham nhũng, phụ thuộc, dự án thiết kế kém lãng phí: quan chức biển thủ, thực phẩm phá chợ nông dân địa phương; nước nhận lâu ngừng xây hệ thống thuế; dự án do nhà tài trợ chọn không hỏi cộng đồng thất bại khi máy hỏng; hỗ trợ sở hữu địa phương: theo dõi, công bố, thiết kế cùng người dùng, đầu tư y tế, giáo dục, hạ tầng; công bằng thương mại, xoá nợ.
Đồng ý nếu nhắm đúng, minh bạch, thiết kế cùng dân địa phương.

essays.question: Do the advantages of free trade outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons and examples.

versions.text:
Many countries have signed agreements that remove tariffs and quotas, and the question is whether the advantages of free trade outweigh the disadvantages. This essay will discuss both sides before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, free trade raises efficiency and consumer choice. Removing tariffs lowers prices and widens markets. A family in a small country that can buy cars from Japan, wine from France and clothing from Vietnam, for example, enjoys far more variety at lower prices than it could if only domestic producers were protected. Exporters can sell to millions of customers abroad, which allows them to grow, to hire more workers and to invest in better technology. Competition forces firms to improve quality and to cut waste, and specialisation lets each country concentrate on what it does best. Many economists believe that open trade has increased global income and lifted millions of people out of poverty.

On the negative side, free trade damages uncompetitive sectors. Domestic industries and workers who cannot compete may collapse, and standards can be undercut. A farming region that faces cheap imported grain, for example, may lose many farms, and the communities that depend on them decline. Countries can become dependent on imported food or medicines, which is dangerous in a crisis. Companies may also move production to places with weak environmental or labour laws. Gains outweigh losses only with adjustment support. Governments should provide retraining, regional investment and temporary assistance for those who lose their jobs, and they should include labour and environmental standards in trade agreements.

In conclusion, free trade brings large benefits in efficiency and choice. On balance, I believe that the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, provided that governments protect those who are harmed by it.

grade.summary: Bài viết có cấu trúc tốt, lập luận rõ ràng và hoàn thành đầy đủ yêu cầu của đề bài về mặt nội dung cũng như độ dài. Ngữ pháp và từ vựng ở mức khá tốt, chỉ cần tinh chỉnh một số lỗi nhỏ để đạt điểm cao hơn.

Một số từ vựng và cụm từ diễn đạt còn khá phổ thông, chưa đạt đến mức độ sắc sảo của band 8.

feedback.taskResponse: Bài viết đã trả lời trực tiếp câu hỏi của đề bài bằng cách phân tích cả lợi ích và bất lợi trước khi đưa ra quan điểm rõ ràng ở phần kết luận. Các luận điểm được phát triển khá tốt với ví dụ cụ thể, tuy nhiên phần giải pháp ở thân bài 3 hơi lấn át phần phân tích bất lợi.
feedback.coherenceCohesion: Bài viết có cấu trúc rõ ràng gồm 4 đoạn tiêu chuẩn, bố cục mạch lạc với các từ nối tốt như 'On the positive side', 'On the negative side', và 'In conclusion'. Các ý trong đoạn được liên kết logic và mượt mà.
feedback.lexicalResource: Sử dụng từ vựng phong phú và phù hợp với chủ đề kinh tế (tariffs, quotas, uncompetitive sectors, specialisation, adjustment support). Tuy nhiên, một số cụm từ chưa thực sự đạt độ tinh tế cao cấp (band 8+).
feedback.grammar: Cấu trúc câu đa dạng, từ câu đơn đến câu phức, ngữ pháp chính xác với rất ít lỗi. Các thì được sử dụng linh hoạt và phù hợp với ngữ cảnh.

analysis.type_vi: A/D: thương mại tự do

plan.think: Mở bài nêu nhiều nước ký hiệp định bỏ thuế, hạn ngạch; kết luận ưu hơn nếu hỗ trợ người bị hại.

Hiệu quả, lựa chọn: bỏ thuế giảm giá, mở thị trường; ví dụ gia đình nước nhỏ mua xe Nhật, rượu Pháp, quần áo Việt Nam đa dạng, giá thấp hơn chỉ bảo hộ sản xuất trong nước; nhà xuất khẩu bán cho hàng triệu khách nước ngoài, thuê thêm, đầu tư công nghệ; cạnh tranh nâng chất lượng, giảm lãng phí; chuyên môn hoá; thu nhập toàn cầu tăng, thoát nghèo.

Hại ngành kém cạnh tranh: ngành nội địa, công nhân sụp đổ, tiêu chuẩn bị hạ; ví dụ vùng nông nghiệp đối mặt gạo, ngũ cốc nhập giá rẻ mất nhiều trang trại, cộng đồng suy; phụ thuộc nhập khẩu thực phẩm, thuốc nguy hiểm khi khủng hoảng; công ty chuyển đến nơi luật lỏng; hỗ trợ chuyển đổi: đào tạo lại, đầu tư vùng, trợ cấp tạm thời, tiêu chuẩn lao động, môi trường trong hiệp định.
Ưu hơn nhược nếu bảo vệ người bị hại.

essays.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of universal basic income.

versions.text:
Several countries have tested the idea of giving every adult a regular payment, whatever their income, and this essay will discuss the advantages and disadvantages of universal basic income before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, universal basic income reduces poverty and insecurity. A guaranteed payment gives everyone a floor, lets people retrain or care for family and replaces complex benefits. A woman who loses her job, for example, can pay for rent and food while she studies for a new career, without waiting for officials to assess her case. Because the money is paid to everyone, there is no stigma and no complicated test, which reduces administration costs and the number of people who fail to claim support. Experiments in Finland and Kenya suggest that recipients often experience less stress and better health. As automation removes some jobs, a basic income could protect people from sudden unemployment and encourage entrepreneurship, since failure is less frightening.

On the negative side, universal basic income is very costly and may weaken work incentives. Paying everyone needs high taxes or cuts in other services, and some of the money goes to people who do not need it. Critics fear that some recipients will work less, though research so far shows small effects. A payment that is too low will not end poverty, while one that is generous may cause inflation, since prices adjust to extra spending power. Pilot schemes should test the effects first. Governments can start with targeted groups or regions, measure the results on jobs, health and spending and then decide whether to expand.

In conclusion, basic income has attractive benefits but serious costs. On balance, I believe that its advantages justify careful testing, although a full national scheme should only follow convincing evidence.

grade.summary: Bài viết nhìn chung đạt chất lượng tốt với lập luận chặt chẽ, từ vựng phù hợp và ngữ pháp chính xác. Để đạt band điểm cao hơn, người viết cần tinh chỉnh một số cấu trúc câu và sử dụng từ vựng mang tính học thuật cao hơn ở phần thảo luận.
weaknesses: Một số ý trong phần thân bài triển khai còn hơi lan man, chưa tối ưu hóa hoàn toàn tính súc tích.
Vài cụm từ diễn đạt có tính văn nói (informal) nhẹ, chưa hoàn toàn trang trọng.

feedback.taskResponse: Bài viết đã trả lời tốt yêu cầu của đề bài bằng cách thảo luận cả ưu điểm và nhược điểm của thu nhập cơ bản phổ thông (UBI), đồng thời đưa ra quan điểm cá nhân rõ ràng. Các ý chính được phát triển khá chi tiết với ví dụ cụ thể.
feedback.coherenceCohesion: Bố cục bài viết mạch lạc, rõ ràng với các phần mở bài, thân bài và kết luận được phân tách tốt. Các từ nối và phương tiện liên kết được sử dụng tự nhiên, giúp người đọc dễ theo dõi lập luận.
feedback.lexicalResource: Vốn từ vựng phong phú và phù hợp với chủ đề kinh tế - xã hội như 'universal basic income', 'stigma', 'administration costs', 'work incentives', 'inflation'. Tuy nhiên, có thể nâng cấp thêm một số cụm từ học thuật để đạt band điểm cao hơn.
feedback.grammar: Cấu trúc câu đa dạng, kết hợp linh hoạt giữa câu đơn, câu ghép và câu phức. Ngữ pháp chính xác, lỗi sai không đáng kể, các thì được sử dụng nhất quán và phù hợp.

analysis.type_vi: A/D: thu nhập cơ bản phổ quát

plan.think: Mở bài nêu một số nước thử trả định kỳ cho mọi người lớn; kết luận cần thử nghiệm thận trọng.

Giảm nghèo, bất an: khoản bảo đảm là nền, cho đào tạo lại, chăm sóc gia đình, thay phúc lợi phức tạp; ví dụ người phụ nữ mất việc trả thuê, ăn trong khi học nghề mới không chờ xét; trả mọi người nên không kỳ thị, không kiểm tra, giảm chi quản lý, số người không xin; thử nghiệm Phần Lan, Kenya ít căng thẳng, khoẻ hơn; tự động hoá, khởi nghiệp.

Rất tốn, có thể yếu động lực làm việc: thuế cao hoặc cắt dịch vụ, tiền đến người không cần; sợ giảm làm việc, nghiên cứu hiệu ứng nhỏ; thấp không hết nghèo, hào phóng lạm phát; thử nghiệm: nhóm, vùng mục tiêu, đo việc làm, sức khoẻ, chi tiêu rồi mở rộng.
Thử nghiệm cẩn thận; chương trình quốc gia sau bằng chứng.

essays.question: Some argue that stricter consumer protection laws improve safety. To what extent do you agree?

versions.text:
Defective toys, contaminated food and faulty electrical goods cause injuries every year, and some argue that stricter consumer protection laws improve safety. I agree to a large extent, since standards and penalties make firms avoid dangerous products, although enforcement matters as much as the laws themselves.

To begin with, stricter consumer protection laws improve safety by setting standards and punishing negligence. Mandatory testing, recalls and heavy fines force firms to avoid dangerous products. A toy manufacturer that must prove its products are free of poisonous paint before selling them, for example, will check its suppliers carefully, since a failure could lead to a ban and a costly lawsuit. Clear labelling of ingredients, allergens and warnings helps buyers to make safe choices, and rules on cooling and hygiene in food production reduce poisoning. Countries with strong consumer agencies, such as those in northern Europe, have lower rates of accidents from household products. When dangerous goods are found, laws allow quick recalls that protect others.

However, compliance costs and weak enforcement can reduce the benefit. Small companies may find the paperwork and testing expensive, which can raise prices or reduce the variety of products, and rules that are not checked are ignored. Online marketplaces make it easy to import cheap goods that avoid inspection. Strong laws with effective inspection protect the public. Governments should fund inspectors and laboratories, hold online platforms responsible for unsafe items sold through them, and cooperate internationally to track dangerous products. Consumers can also help by reporting problems and by reading labels carefully.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that stricter consumer protection laws improve safety, provided that they are enforced and designed with small businesses in mind.

grade.summary: Bài viết của bạn đạt chất lượng tốt, triển khai ý tưởng logic, từ vựng và ngữ pháp chắc tay. Cần chú ý hơn đến việc cân bằng giữa các ý kiến đối lập để bài viết toàn diện hơn.
weaknesses: Đoạn thân bài thứ hai ôm đồm quá nhiều ý (vừa nói về chi phí của doanh nghiệp nhỏ, vừa nói về thị trường trực tuyến, vừa đưa ra giải pháp), làm phân tán trọng tâm.
Phần kết luận lặp lại nguyên văn ý từ mở bài mà chưa tổng hợp lại một cách mới mẻ hơn.

feedback.taskResponse: Bài viết trả lời tốt câu hỏi theo hướng đồng ý phần lớn (agree to a large extent), có thảo luận cả khía cạnh luật pháp và mặt trái/điều kiện đi kèm như chi phí tuân thủ hay thực thi luật. Lập luận rõ ràng và có ví dụ minh họa.
feedback.coherenceCohesion: Bố cục bài viết rất mạch lạc với cấu trúc 4 đoạn chuẩn mực. Các từ nối và phương tiện liên kết được sử dụng tự nhiên, chuyển ý giữa các đoạn mượt mà.
